title: The seven (Acts 6:1–7)
hookLine: widows are neglected, and seven are chosen to serve tables

cards: A church, a school, a family business: at first everyone knows everyone, and things just get done. Then it doubles.
Someone gets forgotten, a complaint starts in the hallway, and it turns out the people on one side of the room have been overlooked.
The early Church in Jerusalem got there fast: a growing community, a daily distribution of food for widows, and two groups who spoke different languages. Someone was being left out.

teach.b: Luke names the two groups: the Hellenists, Jewish believers who spoke Greek, many probably from abroad, and the Hebrews, who spoke Aramaic and were from the land.
The Greek-speaking widows were being neglected in the daily ministration, the daily serving of food. Luke doesn't hide the complaint.
The twelve call everyone together and say, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables." That's not snobbery about waiting tables.
It's honesty about limits: they can't do everything well.
So they ask the community to pick seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, to take charge of it, while the apostles keep to prayer and the ministry of the word.

A detail worth noticing: all seven have Greek names. Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a convert from Antioch. The overlooked group gets leaders who know it from the inside.
The apostles pray and lay their hands on them, and the word of God grows; the number of disciples multiplies greatly.

Deacon comes from the Greek diakonos, a servant, and Luke's word for that daily serving, diakonia, is the same family. Acts never actually calls the seven deacons, but Catholic tradition has long seen them as the first.
Today a deacon is ordained; he proclaims the Gospel at Mass, baptizes, witnesses marriages, leads funerals, and is meant above all to serve the poor.
Stephen, the first named, would soon be killed for his witness; tradition calls him the first martyr.

how: In the Catholic Church deacons are ordained by a bishop; at Mass they proclaim the Gospel, and they may baptize, witness marriages and lead funerals, with a special charge to serve the poor.

o: a monk who lives apart to pray for others
a lay reader who proclaims the readings at Mass
one ordained to serve, from the Greek for servant

p: not leave the word of God to serve tables

s: Acts explicitly calls the seven deacons
it uses the word for serving, diakonia; tradition sees them as the first deacons.
all seven chosen have Greek names
Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolas.
the apostles thought serving tables was beneath them
they named a real limit: they couldn't also leave the word and prayer.

games.q: you're one of the twelve. the Greek-speaking widows are being missed in the daily food, and you can't do it all. what do you do?
o: ask the community to choose seven to serve.
tell the widows to be patient.
games.why: the community chooses seven, all with Greek names, and the apostles pray and lay hands on them. the word of God grows.

practice: If you know a deacon, bring him to mind; if not, think of whoever quietly serves the tables where you are: the volunteer at the food pantry, the person who sets up chairs, the nurse on the night shift.
Then think of anyone around you who might be overlooked, the way those widows were. If you pray, pray for a deacon, or for them; if you don't, just hold them with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Deacon. From the Greek diakonos, a servant: the ministry the Church traces to the seven chosen to serve tables in Acts. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: servant, minister, the root of deacon; Acts 6 uses its cousins diakonia and diakonein.

carryVoice: Your line: serve the tables. Tomorrow, one of the seven takes a desert road. That's day five hundred forty-one.

sources.q: It is not reason that we should leave the word of God, and serve tables.
